results.description: In 1996, a handful of cattle ranchers make a bold decision: to sue IBP, the biggest beef processor in the world. They accuse IBP of price-fixing, putting cattle producers out of business while raising prices for consumers. But the ranchers will soon learn that their fight with Big Beef has actually been raging for decades, involving antitrust crusaders in the 1920s and New York mobsters in the 1970s. results.description: A lot has changed in the eight years since the ranchers first sued Big Beef. IBP was acquired by Tyson Foods, a behemoth with even more ability to withstand a lawsuit. But no sooner does Tyson take the crown as world’s biggest meatpacker than a new heavyweight emerges: Brazil’s JBS. Founded as a family-owned business in the 1950s, JBS is now run by the billionaire Batista brothers, Joesley and Wesley. results.description: It’s early 2020, and COVID-19 is tearing through the world’s meatpacking plants at an alarming pace. Years of consolidation have produced vast quantities of retail-ready meat, and enormous profits for meatpacking conglomerates. But it’s also made them vulnerable to sudden disruption — like a pandemic. results.description:
The U.S. consumes more beef annually than any other country in the world. But if you’ve been to the grocery store lately, you might have experienced some sticker shock. Beef prices have hit all-time highs in recent years. Joining David to unpack the state of the beef industry is Chloe Sorvino, a staff writer at Forbes covering food and agriculture, and author of _Raw Deal: Hidden Corruption, Corporate Greed, and the Fight for the Future of Meat. _They’ll discuss the forces driving high prices for consumers, recent scandals at JBS, concerns over food safety, and what the new generation of ranchers is doing to make meat more sustainable.
